title: Lot Sampling, Sample Identity and Representativeness

content.overview: A laboratory result describes the sample tested. Quality assurance must therefore establish how that sample relates to the larger lot and protect its identity from collection through result review.

vocabulary.definition: A defined quantity of material produced or handled under a common traceable identity.
Documented possession and transfer history of a sample.
A sample created by combining material from multiple defined subsamples.

sections.title: Define the lot before sampling
sections.body: Sampling cannot be representative if the target population is undefined. Record boundaries such as harvest group, cultivar, drying batch and storage condition.

sections.title: Sample across meaningful variation
sections.body: Flower size, container, rack, canopy origin or drying position may create heterogeneity. A plan should identify which sources of variation need representation.

sections.title: Identity must survive every handoff
sections.body: Use unique sample IDs and documented collection, storage and transfer so a result can be tied back to the correct lot.

workedExamples: A sample taken only from the top of one bin may miss wetter material elsewhere in the lot.
A precise lab result with a broken sample ID trail is not strong lot-level evidence.
commonMistakes: Relabeling samples without retaining the original identifier.
content.practicalApplication: Write a sampling map specifying lot definition, subsample locations, amount, sample ID, collector, time and transfer conditions.
content.summary: Representative QA begins before the laboratory: lot definition, sampling design and identity control determine what the result can support.
